newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge to consider sanctions on Prudential.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge to consider sanctions on Prudential.

text.p: U.S. district judge Alfred Wolin will consider at a hearing Wednesday morning whether to impose sanctions on Prudential Insurance Co of America due to the alleged wrongful destruction of documents earlier this year.

Melvyn Weiss, a lead attorney representing policyholders in the class action against Prudential for improper sales practices, said he requested the sanctions after Prudential disclosed the document destruction to him on Saturday.
Prudential was not immediately available for comment.

Prudential officials told the New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance at a meeting on Monday that they discovered the document destruction during a routine compliance examination of its Cambridge, Mass., office.

Documents that were removed and destroyed included marketing material not approved by the company as well as other documents which could be relevant to policyholder claims against the company, the New Jersey insurance department said.

Prudential officials told New Jersey regulators that the company has reviewed 17 of its 19 New Jersey offices and that no such activity appears to have taken place in New Jersey, the insurance department said.
The reports regarding the remaining two New Jersey offices will be complete within the next two weeks, the insurance department said.

Prudential also faces the threat of sanctions in Florida, including the possible loss of its license to operate in that state, after the state insurance commissioner last week charged the company with obstructing a state probe into its sales practices.
Florida insurance commissioner Bill Nelson filed a formal administrative complaint alleging the company obstructed the investigation, destroyed documents and ignored subpoenas.
Earlier this year, Prudential reached an agreement with 43 other states to pay a record $35 million fine to settle allegations of improper sales practices.
The agreement also called for Prudential to reimburse customers nationwide.
The company also has agreed to pay at least $410 million to settle a class action lawsuit over its sales practices.
